In this World Cup finals tournament, over 23% of players—nearly a quarter—were not born in the country they represent, with both the proportion and number hitting historic highs. Among the 48 participating teams, eight squads have a majority of their players born abroad. Curaçao, a constituent country of the Dutch Caribbean, has a population smaller than even Wan Chai, and the entire squad has only one player born locally: Tahith Chong, the most marketable player on the team, a Guangdong descendant developed by Sheffield United; all other players come from the Netherlands itself. The stark mismatch between strong and weak teams facing off at the World Cup is reflected not only in the viewing experience for fans but also in the dilemma facing football associations, which struggle to boost attention by featuring both marquee stars and minnow nations. This tournament has been plagued by controversy: fans mock the heavily promoted stars as "FIFA Boys," and multiple team representatives have lodged complaints with the federation over officiating standards after matches. For fans, when they look back on the classic matches of the 2026 World Cup years from now, the one that may stand out might not be the final, but the round-of-16 thriller in which defending champions Argentina edged Cape Verde 3–2. Vozinha, a 40-year-old obscure Cape Verdean goalkeeper, pulled off a string of saves against Lionel Messi's shots and became an overnight sensation, now boasting nearly 30 million followers worldwide. On the eve of the previous World Cup, the federation wrote to all participating teams, pleading for "let football be the protagonist" and urging that the game not be drawn into any ideological or political struggles. At that time, the World Cup was still hosted by a single country, with 32 national teams taking part. The next World Cup will mark its centenary and will, in an unprecedented move, span three continents and six host nations.
